    Callout

    All instructor pages

    These live under the Extras dropdown, which the site shows only when the Instructor View toggle (top bar) is on.

    • Account preparation checklist (quotas, Bedrock, tags): before the term. As of October 2026 the notebook role ml-sagemaker-use carries two inline policies set from CloudShell: BedrockAccess, so any instance can call Bedrock, and WorkshopGuardRails, which refuses untagged, blank-tagged or placeholder-tagged jobs, instance types outside the lesson’s list, endpoints and EC2. Both are on that page with the command that applies them; the guard rails are not yet on the learner permission set.
    • Shared data bucket: staging before each term: create and fill ml-marathon-shared from CloudShell.
    • Badger Scribe data: publishing a release: only when the competition data changes.
    • Fine-tuning episode: cost, capacity and setup
    • This page: cleaning the account with aws-nuke after the workshop. The config it uses is instructors/nuke-config.yml in the repository.

    Hello all! In this document, we will show you how to run an AWS Nuke script within the ML-Marathon Sagemaker server. As you progress through the Sagemaker workshop, towards the end of the workshop you’ll be tasked to remove and empty your notebooks & buckets. However, depending on the size of your data, it can take a long time to remove them altogether.

    This is where the AWS Nuke script comes in handy, instead of removing your notebooks and buckets one-by-one, the script automates this process and removes it for you!

    Here are the following steps on how to launch and run the AWS-Nuke Script:

    1. Open CloudShell in the correct AWS account

    1. Sign in to the AWS Console for the account you intend to clean.
    2. In the top-right Region, select the Region where you want CloudShell storage to live. In this case, we will choose US-East-2 (OHIO) since that’s where we store our servers.
    3. Open CloudShell from the console toolbar.
    4. Verify exactly which account/role you are using:

    BASH 

    aws sts get-caller-identity

    2. Get the config file into CloudShell

    aws-nuke needs a config file in .yml or .yaml format or else your script will FAIL. The one for this workshop is committed in the lesson repository at instructors/nuke-config.yml. Two things it deliberately does not delete: the shared data bucket (the filters block) and Bedrock application inference profiles, which learners remove themselves in the cleanup episode. Everything else the lesson creates (training, processing and tuning jobs) has already ended and holds no billable resource.

    Download it straight into CloudShell and check it:

    BASH 

    curl -fsSL -o "$HOME/nuke-config.yml" https://raw.githubusercontent.com/carpentries-incubator/ML_with_AWS_SageMaker/main/instructors/nuke-config.yml
cat "$HOME/nuke-config.yml"

    If you need to change it (a different account ID, another bucket to keep), edit the file in CloudShell with nano "$HOME/nuke-config.yml", or edit a copy on your own machine and upload it with “Actions” > “Upload file”. Use space indenting, not tabs: YAML is sensitive to this and the script will fail on tabs.

    3. Download and install the linux version

    AWS CloudShell uses Linux as their base distribution. So you will need to download the linux version of AWS Nuke from Github. You should download only from the official ekristen/aws-nuke releases, not use any local version.

    Link: https://github.com/ekristen/aws-nuke/releases

    Run the following:

    BASH 

    mkdir -p "$HOME/bin"
cd "$HOME"
curl -fL -o aws-nuke-v3.67.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz \
  https://github.com/ekristen/aws-nuke/releases/download/v3.67.0/aws-nuke-v3.67.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
tar -xzf aws-nuke-v3.67.0-linux-amd64.tar.gz
mv aws-nuke "$HOME/bin/aws-nuke"
chmod 700 "$HOME/bin/aws-nuke"
export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"
aws-nuke --version

    To make aws-nuke stay on your PATH in later CloudShell sessions:

    BASH 

    echo 'export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

    Reminder: CloudShell is based on Amazon Linux, and software saved in $HOME persists; software installed elsewhere may disappear after the session ends.

    4. DO a dry run first

    It is important that you first run a dry-run so that you can verify which files you want to remove before executing the actual script.

    Here is the script to do so:

    BASH 

    aws-nuke run --config "$HOME/nuke-config.yml"

    This should list resources it would remove, without deleting them. Review the output carefully, especially S3 buckets, IAM-related resources, and the displayed account identity.

    5. Only after review: actual deletion

    Only if the dry-run output is correct and this is truly the intended non-production account:

    BASH 

    aws-nuke run --config "$HOME/nuke-config.yml" --no-dry-run

    Do not add --no-prompt / --force on your first real run; leave the confirmation prompt enabled as an additional safeguard.

    If the dry run stops on “account doesn’t have an alias”

    Oftentimes when running the dry run, you will run into an error stating:

    WARN[0000] 'targets' is deprecated. Please use 'includes' instead.
aws-nuke - v3.67.0 - 9cc98ccaed6303dac29001642879320ab584d41a
FATA[0000] specified account doesn't have an alias. For safety reasons you need
to specify an account alias. Your production account should contain the term 'prod'

    Do not panic, this isn’t related to CloudShell or credentials. Rather, it connected to AWS successfully but stopped abruptly since the account you are trying to target has no AWS account alias. By default, aws-nuke requires an alias so you must visually confirm a recognizable account name before proceeding. It also blocks aliases containing prod by default.

    Recommended: create a non-production account alias. First, verify the exact account:

    BASH 

    aws sts get-caller-identity

    Then add an alias in the AWS Console:

    1. Go to IAM
    2. Open Dashboard
    3. Under AWS Account, choose Create Alias
    4. Set a clear, unique non-production alias, e.g. mycompany-sandbox or training-cleanup
    5. Do not use a name containing prod, production, or live.

    Then run the dry-run again:

    BASH 

    aws-nuke run --config "$HOME/nuke-config.yml"

    Congratulations, you have reached the end of this tutorial! By now, all scripts should work and the specified notebooks/buckets you wanted to clean should now be all empty!

    Before class (instructor checklist)

    Students never download the data themselves; four things have to be in place before the session. Each is written out in the instructor pages.

    1. Stage the data in the shared read-only bucket from the lesson’s data release (badger-scribe-data-v1, ~130 MB): a few minutes from CloudShell, a laptop or a notebook instance; commands and the read-only bucket policy in Shared data bucket: staging before each term (the same bucket holds the WattBot data for the RAG episodes). The bucket must survive the end-of-workshop cleanup, or be recreated from the release next term.
    2. Stage the base model in the same bucket (badger-scribe/model/churro-3B/, ~7.5 GB, once, from a laptop or notebook instance, not CloudShell). Every job reads the weights from S3 as a model channel instead of 100 students pulling 7.5 GB each from Hugging Face in the same minute.
    3. Quotas: ml.g5.xlarge for training job usage at least the class size (request 100). Default is often 0 to 4 and increases take days; file three to four weeks ahead. Full list in Account preparation checklist.
    4. Keep the bucket name ml-marathon-shared; the episodes have it filled in. If you stage under another name, tell students to change shared_bucket in the first code cell.

    Fallback instance if g5 capacity is short: ml.g6.xlarge (L4, 24 GB, $1.13/h).
